items.title: S&P 500 Futures Rise After Tough Week
items.summary: Early investor bets pointed to some stability when regular trading resumes on Monday, though analysts warned that more volatility could still be ahead.
items.full_text:
Title: S&P 500 Futures Rise After Tough Week - The New York Times

URL Source: https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/22/business/ai-stocks-sp500.html

Published Time: Mon, 23 Nov 2026 01:50:16 GMT

Markdown Content:
Early trading signals on Sunday night pointed to the return of some stability when stock exchanges reopen on Monday morning, after major indexes fell sharply last week as concerns over the artificial intelligence industry spilled into a broader market rout.

Futures on the S&P 500, which allow investors to make early bets on the stock market, rose roughly 2 percent as trading got underway on Sunday evening. The rise came after the index slumped 8.6 percent last week, its worst weekly performance since President Trump announced his sweeping global tariffs in April 2025.

The early sign of stability on Sunday night is likely to be welcomed by investors who have spent weeks buffeted by sharp price swings in some of the most widely owned stocks in the market.

Last week’s drop left the index in what traders call “correction” territory, defined as a fall of 10 percent or more from a stock or index’s recent peak. Such a steep decline denotes a significant amount of strain in the market. The S&P 500 has now fallen over 11 percent since its high at the start of October, erasing most of its earlier gain through the first nine months of the year.

But while many analysts and investors remain bullish about the path ahead, expecting the stock market to recover at least some ground before the end of the year, many also expected the big swings in stock prices to continue.

The stock market’s sharp fall last week came despite a record-breaking entry into the stock market for Anthropic, one the A.I. industry’s pioneers, and a bumper profit report for Nvidia, which at one point was the most highly valued company in the world. Over the last six weeks, though, it has lost nearly half its value.

“The headwinds have grown stronger,” Stuart Kaiser, head of equity trading strategy at Citi, said. He referred to last week’s sell-off as a “gut-punch” after neither Nvidia’s earnings nor Anthropic’s market debut were able to stop the sell-off.

Investors’ doubts remain about the ability for some large A.I. companies to keep growing quickly enough to justify their previously lofty share prices. Many of those companies have also turned to debt markets to fund their spending, with debt investors steadily demanding higher interest rates to keep lending to them. There is also the prospect of tougher regulations, both in exports of A.I. chips to China and in construction of new data centers.

Some analysts suggested the sell-off in recent weeks had been made worse by so much of the market looking at the same time to lower its exposure to the A.I. industry. Some also noted that the unwinding of the A.I. trade had not yet run its course.

“We don’t think we’re there yet,” noted Jeffrey Favuzza, an analyst who sits on the equity trading desk at the investment bank Jefferies. He was referring to mutual and pension funds reducing their holdings of A.I. stocks to match the indexes they are benchmarked to.

The financial markets will be closed for the Thanksgiving holiday, and trading volumes are typically subdued for the entire week. That can lead to abrupt changes in stock prices. Retail investors have also been less willing to step in and buy stocks that have fallen sharply in price. Investors buying those dips had helped the market recover from declines at the start of the Iran war in March and last year when Mr. Trump rolled out his tariff proposals.

“The market is questioning whether today’s spending will generate the profits investors had assumed, who will ultimately capture those profits and whether the A.I. earnings cycle is approaching a peak,” said Keith Lerner, chief market strategist at Truist Wealth. “Until investors have better visibility, they are selling first and asking questions later.”

items.title: How Six Americans Under 40 Are Saving for Retirement
items.summary: Whether they take a traditional path or go their own way, some younger workers are managing to build a nest egg while juggling other financial challenges.
items.full_text:
Title: How Six Americans Under 40 Are Saving for Retirement - The New York Times

URL Source: https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/22/business/retirement-millennials-gen-z.html

Published Time: Mon, 23 Nov 2026 02:01:15 GMT

Markdown Content:
The old paradigm of getting a steady job, buying a home by age 30 — or ever — and building a career with one employer has all but crumbled.

But in Americans’ personal finances, one thing hasn’t changed: the need to save for retirement. Because they are juggling student loan debts and health care costs, many younger workers find doing that almost impossible. Yet some millennials and members of Generation Z are finding ways to save, even if that means making hard choices or rejecting experts’ advice.

The New York Times spoke with six adults under 40, who are all single and don’t have children, about their financial priorities and their methods of saving and investing for their later years.

## She wants to feel in control

![Image 1](https://static01.nyt.com/images/2026/11/17/multimedia/00bizsun-retiring-save-01-v2-kqfw/00bizsun-retiring-save-01-v2-kqfw-jumbo.jpg)Credit...Taylor Ballek for The New York Times

“If your priorities look different from people that are older in your life, trust your instincts to take a different path.”

Zayda Slabbekoorn

Zayda Slabbekoorn has two big financial goals: save for retirement and build an emergency fund. She invests 5 percent of her salary in a 401(k) plan at work, but right now the emergency fund is taking the front seat.

So she aims to save $10,000 in cash in case she’s laid off as an editorial strategist or decides to move away from Grand Rapids, Mich.

Each month, $600 is automatically deducted from her paycheck and put into a high-yield savings account toward that emergency fund. Any excess — typically about $100 a month — also goes there. “I want to feel like I have control over my financial situation as much as possible,” she said. At a previous job, Ms. Slabbekoorn, 24, put 8 percent into her 401(k) and received an employer match. She no longer has a match, and doesn’t feel as comfortable putting that much in a retirement plan without it.

“I feel like my money is better located in a savings account that I can access without having to take any kind of penalty” for withdrawing it, she said.

Once she builds the emergency fund, Ms. Slabbekoorn said, she will consider bumping up her retirement savings and paying down her student loan debt more aggressively — at the moment, she is paying the minimum $700 monthly on an $80,000 balance. She freelances to make extra money.

Her father gives her advice, but it doesn’t always align with her goals, she said. When her parents were her age, they were married with a mortgage and plans for a family. But she isn’t sketching out that kind of future and has stopped comparing herself with her parents.

## He didn’t know enough to start saving

![Image 2](https://static01.nyt.com/images/2026/11/17/multimedia/00bizsun-retiring-save-02-v2-hpbc/00bizsun-retiring-save-02-v2-hpbc-jumbo.jpg)Credit...Oliver Farshi for The New York Times

“I feel like I’m controlling the things I can control, and there’s not much more I can do.”

Rayshawn Whitford

Rayshawn Whitford, 36, bought a house in Woodbridge, Conn., this year. His mortgage consumes 25 percent of his gross income, and he no longer has student loan debt, having paid it off several years after college, so he’s in a position to save.

Mr. Whitford maxes out his 401(k) each year and receives a match from the nonprofit foundation where he is an operations director, but he didn’t start saving there until he was 29, which he regrets.

“My first job, where I was making good money, I didn’t know enough to start saving,” said Mr. Whitford, who hadn’t thought he would stay at the company long enough to become vested in its plan. “So I thought, why put money into what I wouldn’t have access to until later?” he said. Now, he budgets for his contribution.

He wants to save $1.5 million by age 55. Yet he wonders if it will be enough, and he isn’t confident Social Security and Medicare will be there for him.

## She opened a Roth I.R.A. at age 14

![Image 3](https://static01.nyt.com/images/2026/11/17/multimedia/00bizsun-retiring-save-03-v2-jwlq/00bizsun-retiring-save-03-v2-jwlq-jumbo.jpg)Credit...Ian C. Bates for The New York Times

“Gen Z has a very nonlinear view of what financial security looks like.”

Amrita Bhasin

Amrita Bhasin, 25, has been using her father’s financial advice since he insisted she open a Roth individual retirement account at 14, when she got her first summer job. Now, she’s an entrepreneur, having co-founded a supply chain software company in San Francisco. At his urging, last November Ms. Bhasin set up a 401(k) plan for the small company and its workers, and she maxes out her own contribution. She’s also the only one using it.

Ms. Bhasin follows her father’s guidance, but she believes that career paths today are less predictable and that Gen Z is likely to take a different financial path than previous generations did.

“Many people feel like they’re not going to be able to afford to buy a house like the one that they grew up in,” Ms. Bhasin said. She questions what financial stability will look like for her generation.

Maxing out a 401(k) can require a level of sacrifice that is difficult for the average person, Ms. Bhasin said. To shore up her finances, she supplements her income with freelance work and, for the past several years, has made an annual plan for spending on vacations, clothes and experiences. “I usually stay pretty close to my annual budget,” she said.

## He’s an owner and a landlord

![Image 4](https://static01.nyt.com/images/2026/11/17/multimedia/00bizsun-retiring-save-04-v3-gzcp/00bizsun-retiring-save-04-v3-gzcp-jumbo.jpg)Credit...Jamie Kelter Davis for The New York Times

“Growing up, my dad and I used to talk about retirement planning and being strategic with the things we do.”

Jabari Washington

Jabari Washington, 25, received a full scholarship to college to study math and actuarial science, graduating with no student loan debt. He also worked throughout school, including at a well-paying internship. That allowed him to save enough to buy a house in Bloomington-Normal, Ill., even before graduating in May 2023. Last year, he bought a second house in town.

It helps, he said, that housing prices where he lives are reasonable (according to [Zillow](https://www.zillow.com/home-values/23742/bloomington-il/), the average home there is about $270,000, lower than the national average). Mr. Washington lives in one of the houses with roommates who pay rent and rents the other house.

How does he manage to do that while also saving separately for retirement? Mr. Washington’s internship led to a career as an actuary, in which he earns six figures. When it comes to retirement savings, he takes a traditional route: He puts 6 percent in a 401(k), receiving a 3 percent employer match.

He also saves $4,400 a year in a health savings account and has three brokerage accounts, two of which he opened in college. One of those accounts holds the money he tithes to his church — 10 percent of his salary. “I’m trying to wean myself off of keeping everything for myself,” Mr. Washington said.

## She skips the 403(b)

![Image 5](https://static01.nyt.com/images/2026/11/17/multimedia/00bizsun-retiring-save-05-v2-cflh/00bizsun-retiring-save-05-v2-cflh-jumbo.jpg)Credit...Alyssa Schukar for The New York Times

“I don’t really understand anything about pensions, to be fully transparent, and I’ve never stayed at a job for five years.”

Alexa Hayes

Alexa Hayes, a graphic designer, prefers having liquid assets to locking up her savings in a workplace plan, so she invests in the stock market directly using a brokerage account. She also considers her Washington, D.C., apartment, which she owns (thanks partly to an inheritance), to be a big piece of her retirement plan. “It’s paid off so, in theory, I can sell it for profit and then invest that income,” she said.

Last year, when Ms. Hayes, 38, lost her federal contractor job, she had to sell $2,000 in stock and use all her cash savings of $25,000 to pay bills while she searched for another role. The hunt took 10 months, and her longstanding freelance work helped.

“It was dire straits, and having that access to money felt much safer than tucking it away in a 401(k),” she said. (She did not qualify for unemployment.)

While out of work, Ms. Hayes deferred payments on the $60,000 she owes in student loans, and since October, has been required to make monthly student loan payments of $665. The interest is a burden, she said. “The daily accrual on student loans is so suffocating, it feels like you are chipping away at a mountain that continues to grow.”

Ms. Hayes was hired at a nonprofit that offers a pension and a 403(b), which is similar to a 401(k). She will be fully vested in the pension in five years and admits she doesn’t fully understand how it works. She doesn’t plan to contribute to the 403(b) this year or next.

## He was a pianist who pivoted to nursing

![Image 6](https://static01.nyt.com/images/2026/11/22/multimedia/22bizsun-retiring-save-retoned-cfhw/22bizsun-retiring-save-retoned-cfhw-jumbo.jpg)Credit...Rebecca Gratz for The New York Times

“When you only pay the minimum, you’re going to be absolutely destroyed by interest.”

Chase Cooper

For the last two years, Chase Cooper, 38, has worked overtime every week so he can keep saving for retirement and have money to socialize with friends and take vacations. He is saving 6 percent of his salary in a 401(k) with an employer match, and last year he began contributing the maximum to a Roth I.R.A.

Mr. Cooper said he didn’t start saving for retirement right away. “I feel like I’m late to the party,” he said.
